blocks.text: i. Combustion of alcohols
Alcohols when ignited, undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.
The above reaction is highly exothermic; this is why the alcohol is used as an alternate to petrol in some countries.
ii. Substitution reaction

In the substitution of alcohols, a hydroxy group (-OH) is replaced by another substituent (e.g. halogens) to form a new product (e.g., halogenoalkanes). The substitution of different halogens with the –OH group is given in the following reactions.

iii. Reaction with sodium metal

When an alcohol reacts with a reactive metal such as sodium (Na), the oxygen-hydrogen bond in the hydroxly group breaks. Though the reaction is less vigorous than sodium reacting with water, hydrogen gas is given off and a base (alkoxide) is formed. This reaction can be used as a test for hydroxy (-OH) group. Bubbles of hydrogen gas are released if a hydroxy group is present. If the excess ethanol is evaporated off after the reaction, a white crystalline solid of sodium alkoxide is left. The longer the hydrocarbon chain in the alcohol, the less vigorous the reaction becomes.

When sodium metal is added to a solution of phenolphthalein and ethanol, pink colour is formed slowly. With water, the pink colour appears immediately. It shows that reaction of Na with ethanol is slower than with water.
iv. Oxidation of alcohols

Primary alcohols can be oxidised to form aldehydes and the secondary alcohols can be oxidised to form only ketones using oxidizing agents. Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation. The oxidising agents for alcohols include acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and acidified KMnO₄. Acidified potassium chromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇, is an orange oxidising agent. When alcohols are oxidised the orange dichromate ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: K₂Cr₂O₇ is potassium dichromate(VI), not potassium chromate(VI) (which is K₂CrO₄), as the book itself names it in the same paragraph and in the Keep in Mind box.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The label under ethanol is printed 'ethonal'; it is ethanol.

blocks.title: Keep in Mind
blocks.text: For potassium dichromate(VI) to act as an oxidising agent, it must first be reduced. This reduction requires hydrogen (H⁺) ions which are provided by the acidic medium.

Therefore, only the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols will change the colour of acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution as the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ions are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions, which is used to check the presence of primary or secondary alcohol.

blocks.alt: Three test tubes of acidified potassium dichromate: propan-1-ol (primary alcohol) dark green, propan-2-ol (secondary alcohol) dark green, and 2-methyl-propan-2-ol (tertiary alcohol) orange.
blocks.caption: Acidified potassium dichromate with primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 94).

blocks.text: Only propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, which are primary and secondary alcohols respectively, can get oxidised, turning the orange solution green; no colour change is observed with 2-methyl-propan-2-ol, which is a tertiary alcohol.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Driving after consuming alcohol is very dangerous. A breathalyser is a device that is used by the traffic officers to check if a driver is drunk or not. This device uses the oxidation of ethanol, which requires electrons. The amount of current used is proportional to the amount of alcohol consumed.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Oxidation releases electrons; it does not require them. In the breathalyser the ethanol in the breath is oxidised, and the electrons it gives up make the current that is measured; the current is proportional to the amount of alcohol.

v. Dehydration of alcohols
Alcohols can also undergo dehydration to form alkenes. Dehydration is the type of the elimination reaction in which a water molecule is removed.

blocks.text: Dehydrating agents may be aluminium oxide, conc. sulphuric, acid, conc phosphoric acid, etc.
